rv.q: Electra/Persona is bold, dazzling, challenging for both actors and audience.
Electra is good, Persona is good, Electra/Persona isn't necessarily one for the ages.
Not a fully successful experiment, then. But, aptly for a piece so keenly focused on performance, the acting is magnificent.
As a double bill, of sorts, the first is the showcase, not only of its two central performers but the power of performance itself.
Watching this hybrid play is often a laborious exercise, like trying to connect pieces from two different jigsaw puzzles that don't quite fit.
It’s not a case of too little too late, but for all its stylishness and persuasive performances, this production is clinically intellectual – theatre for the head, not the heart.
As theatre, though, it lacks spontaneity.
His previous shows in London have been revelatory. This one is a misstep.
At first intrigued by the shenanigans from ancient myth, I simply lost patience with the muddle of existential angst.
As a piece of theatre, Electra/Persona may not knit together, but it’s powerfully absorbing.
That ultimately leaves Electra/Persona as a fascinating and commanding watch, though slightly sterile.
The production’s real strength is in the elegant parallels it draws, to form a new whole that enriches and enhances the work of both Sophocles and Bergman.
It's an odd night of theatre, but their presence makes it a thrilling one.
Ultimately then, a stylish piece which is well-acted, cleverly crafted and slickly presented.
Electra is emotionally astute and nuanced.

However, the omission of all but four characters certainly gives Andrews' staging great impetus, enabling the audience to concentrate on the main protagonists; at times it is quite gripping, even if the momentum is not sustained throughout.
It is not a simple double bill but a singular, enthralling work of art that lingers long after the final bow.
Andrews has achieved through his adaptation and direction is nothing short of impressive, matched and possibly even surpassed by the exceptional performances from Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss.
Electra/Persona is an intense, strange, compelling hybrid: measured but pacy; part cinema, part theatre; pretentious but emotionally accessible, too.
Savour Electra though – because it's visually arresting and Blanchett and Hoss conjure up literal theatrical sparks of electricity.
If this daring experiment doesn’t quite come off, it’s still a compelling piece of theatre that boasts stellar performances from Cate Blanchett and Nina Hoss in alternating roles.
Andrews beautifully rethinks Sophocles but proves unequal to Bergman.
Ultimately, Blanchett and Hoss delivered a performance for the ages – but the same couldn't be said for the script.
The effect of Andrews’s writing and direction is deeply contradictory: this is both cerebral and emotional; compelling and distancing; fascinating and a bit banal.
Electra / Persona is a challenging piece to explain and to experience.
Make no mistake, Electra/Persona is excellently staged, with strong performances, but ironically, for a play about individuality, this double bill struggles to coalesce.
Electra/Persona is a long and plodding journey without any particular destination, albeit one with moments of real beauty along the way.
Benedict Andrews gave birth to master play.
Electra/Persona is a psychologically engaging production, reaching back to Ancient Greece via Bergman and into the present day.
It might just be worth seeing for the two lead actors at the height of their on-stage and – as this production surprisingly proves – on-screen powers.

By the end (of what felt like forever), I couldn't have cared less about these characters and that really isn't an ideal outcome for a theatre show, which should leave you thinking and questioning but not scratching your head in boredom.
But the production as a whole is easier to admire than to feel: intellectually alive, only fitfully moving, and, for all its ambition, never quite captivating.

cn.t: Blanchett and Hoss deliver magnetic performances in this ambitious but uneven fusion of Sophocles and Bergman. Critics praise the acting prowess and bold concept, though many find the mashup intellectually muddled and dramatically incoherent.
